lines: Avery Brooks
+1 (555) 010-3319 | avery.brooks@example.com | example.com/in/abrooks
Date of birth: 9 Jan 1998 | Nationality: Brazilian
EDUCATION
Eastmoor University | B.S. in Statistics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2016 - May 2020
EXPERIENCE
Brightcart Retail | Data Analyst | Metro City, USA | Aug 2022 - Jun 2025
- Built the weekly retention dashboard for 2.4M customers that marketing used to retarget lapsed buyers, lifting 90-day repeat purchase from 22% to 27%.
- Cut the monthly revenue report from 3 days of spreadsheet work to 2 hours by moving it to scheduled SQL queries and a shared dashboard.
- Found customers with no orders by left-joining the orders table to the customers table and counting rows with a null customer name.

- Joining 40 source tables, deduplicating customer records across two loyalty systems and rebuilding the attribution logic in dbt-style SQL models, raised the share of orders tied to a campaign from 58% to 81%.
- Presented the quarterly customer review to the leadership team, and two of its three recommendations were funded in the next budget.
- Trained 20 merchandisers to answer their own questions with the self-serve dashboards, halving ad hoc data requests.
Pinecrest Insurance | Junior Analyst | Metro City, USA | Apr 2021 - Jul 2022
- Ran the checkout A/B test until significance by checking the p-value every day and stopping on the first day it fell below 0.05.
- Analyzed 18 months of call-center data; the findings moved two agents to the evening peak and cut average hold time from 9 to 5 minutes.
- Wrote the team's SQL style guide and review checklist, which cut query errors found in review by half.

- Automated the monthly fraud-flag extract while also maintaining the team calendar, answering ad hoc questions from sales, updating onboarding documents and covering the help desk on Fridays, which saved the fraud team 10 hours a month.
PROJECTS
City Bike-Share Demand Study | Independent Project | Python, SQL | Jan 2025 - Present
- Leveraged data-driven insights and advanced analytics to unlock actionable value for urban mobility stakeholders.
- Cut empty-station hours from 300 to 200 a week, a 50% reduction, in a replay of last summer's rebalancing.
- Raised forecast hit rate by 15% across 120 stations, from 60% to 75%, by adding weather and event features.
Food Pantry Visit Analysis | Volunteer, Team of 3 | Excel, SQL | Mar 2023 - Aug 2023
- Mapped 14 months of pantry visits by hour and day, so the pantry moved one volunteer shift and cut the Saturday line from 50 to 20 minutes.
- 9,000 handwritten visit logs were cleaned into a single table and repeat visitors were matched, so the pantry had its first count of unique households.
- Wrote a one-page guide the pantry coordinator used to update the visit table each month after the project ended.
SKILLS
Tools: SQL, Python, Excel
Methods: dashboards, forecasting, metric design, data-quality checks

items.says: The résumé includes a date of birth and nationality, personal details conventionally left off.
items.because: A reader is not meant to weigh them when assessing qualifications, and they use space without strengthening the evidence.

items.says: Experience should appear ahead of Education.
items.because: With two analytics roles listed, work history is the clearest evidence of your current direction.

items.says: The résumé shows a 10-month gap between the degree ending and the first listed role.
The stated join cannot identify customers with no orders.
items.because: With orders as the left table, it preserves orders; a null customer name does not necessarily indicate a customer without orders.

items.says: The line gives no business outcome for finding customers with no orders.
items.because: It does not show what action or decision the finding supported.

items.says: The result is buried after a long list of methods.
items.because: A reader reaches several methods before seeing the change from 58% to 81%.

items.says: A comma incorrectly separates the subject from its verb.
items.because: The comma after “models” breaks the sentence between its subject and verb.

items.says: The line names the presentation but not the analysis behind its recommendations.
items.because: Without the analytical contribution, the funded recommendations are harder to connect to your work.

items.says: Repeated p-value checking and stopping below 0.05 do not justify calling the result significant at the usual 5% level.
items.because: That stopping rule increases the false-positive rate above 5%.

items.says: The bullet emphasizes the stopping procedure rather than what the test changed.
items.because: Without the checkout metric and result, a reader cannot judge the test’s usefulness.

items.says: The line does not say what analysis revealed the evening peak.
items.because: The basis for the staffing recommendation is unclear.

items.says: The strongest line in the Pinecrest entry is not the opening one.
items.because: Opening with the call-center analysis would make its measured impact easier to notice.

items.says: A long list of unrelated duties separates the automation from its result.
items.because: The intervening responsibilities make the 10-hour monthly saving harder to spot and do not explain it.

items.says: The Pinecrest entry reads as a collection of testing, operations, and process improvements rather than a clear progression.
items.because: The sequence does not make the relationship among that work clear.

items.says: The bullet uses vague claims without naming the work performed or a concrete outcome.
items.because: The phrases could describe many projects, and the claim of value names no action, decision, or result.

items.says: The decrease from 300 to 200 hours is a 33⅓% reduction, not 50%.
items.because: The decrease of 100 hours is one-third of the 300-hour baseline.

items.says: The line does not name the rebalancing approach tested in the replay.
items.because: Without the approach, a reader cannot see what choice produced the result.

items.says: The strongest line in the project is not the opening one.
items.because: Leading with the concrete empty-station result would make it easier to find.

items.says: The change from 60% to 75% is 15 percentage points, not a 15% relative increase.
items.because: The before-and-after rates differ by 15 percentage points; a relative increase means something different.

items.says: The result is delayed after the method and timeframe.
The line omits the number of unique households identified.
items.because: The count is the clearest measure of what the analysis uncovered.

items.says: The passive phrasing hides your actions.
items.because: “Were cleaned” and “were matched” leave your contribution unclear.

items.says: The matching method is not explained.
items.because: Matching is central to producing a unique-household count.

items.says: The outcome is delayed after the process description.
items.because: Placing the first count of unique households first would make it easier to spot.

items.says: The line does not say what the monthly updates improved.
